newsitem.title: ITALY: European ministers reassure Turkey but seek action.
newsitem.headline: European ministers reassure Turkey but seek action.

text.p: Europe's "big five" powers told Turkey on Wednesday that it had every right to aspire to full membership of the European Union but must make progress on human rights, the Kurdish issue and its disputes with Greece.

Foreign ministers from Britain, France, Germany, Spain and Italy met Turkey's Tansu Ciller to review ties amid tensions over Cyprus and signals from Ankara that it could veto NATO expansion plans if its EU aspirations remain frustrated.

They made clear that they had delivered a strong message to Ciller, who is also deputy prime minister in the Islamist-led government, that Turkey should continue to look to Europe, rather than shift towards its Moslem neighbours.
"We have an enormous interest in making sure that Turkey feels that Europe is not indifferent to which way Turkey turns," Germany's Klaus Kinkel said. "We want Turkey with us."

But Kinkel and other ministers said progress on territorial disputes with Greece and the Cyprus stand-off as well as improvements in human rights and the situation of Kurds had to be achieved before Turkey could become a full EU member.

French Foreign Minister Herve De Charette said there were "no obstacles in principle" to a future EU place but that the outstanding issues "naturally represent difficulties on the path to Turkey's possible membership".
Ciller used a speech on the eve of the meeting to hit home Turkey's frustration at what it considers its "second rate" relationship with the 15-nation EU.
Bemoaning commitments to 11 other countries that they could aspire to EU membership, she said the matter of Turkey's exclusion could no longer be separated from NATO enlargement.

She signalled that Ankara, a founder member of NATO and key strategic ally of the West, could veto plans by the military alliance to expand into former communist states unless the EU delivered on closer ties.
"How do you think you can expand NATO without Turkey's permission?" Ciller asked.
She told a news conference that Wednesday's informal talks had shown that Turkey would not be overlooked for EU membership.
"I am very happy as far as the results of today's meeting are concerned that the same criteria and the same standards will be (applied) to Turkey as to the other 11 countries," she said.
EU diplomats have privately expressed annoyance at Greece's position on Turkey, which has contributed to a block on aid due to flow to Ankara under a customs union signed in 1996.
Kinkel noted that Turkey was "disappointed and frustrated" while British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said Ankara's present relationship with the EU was "unsatisfactory".
"We believe Turkey should be treated in the same way as other applicant countries," Rifkind said.

They and other ministers said they had urged to Turkey, as they have to Greece, to resolve territorial disputes in the Aegean through negotiation and put pressure on their respective kin on divided Cyprus to work towards a settlement.
The search for a solution has been complicated by Greek Cypriot government plans to deploy Russian anti-aircraft missiles and Turkish threats of military retaliation.

Rifkind said Britain, the former colonial power on the island, regretted the attitude of both sides in the dispute and called for "proper negotiations...this year with a view to major progress" on the island's future.
Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkey invaded and occupied the northern third of the island after a Greek Cypriot coup engineered by Greece's then military junta.
